# ADR-0003: Permissive libraries, copyleft application

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-29

**References:** [RFC-0001:C-CONTRIB](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-contrib), [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license)

## Context

The initial inclination was AGPL-3.0 throughout, libraries included. That came from the copyleft
culture of the tools Strider is positioned against — QGIS and CloudCompare are both GPL-2.0-or-later
— rather than from any commercial concern.

Examining who would actually adopt the library crates showed the cost. PDAL is BSD-3-Clause and GDAL
is MIT; neither can link copyleft code at all. QGIS and CloudCompare are GPL-2.0-or-later, and
**AGPL-3.0 is incompatible with GPL-2.0** — so a tool positioned as "the QGIS of point clouds" would
be one QGIS itself could never call. Every commercial forestry product is likewise excluded. Copyleft
libraries would be adoptable by less than half of the ecosystem they were written for, and the
excluded half contains precisely the projects whose adoption would turn the format adapters and
spatial access layer into shared infrastructure rather than duplicated effort.

AGPL's distinguishing feature is also inert here: its network-use clause triggers when users interact
with the software over a network, and a desktop workbench has no such interaction. The full adoption
cost would be paid to close a loophole the software does not have.

Four library licences were assessed.

**Apache-2.0 with MIT as an alternative** is the Rust ecosystem default and permits adoption by every
tool considered. Apache-2.0 alone is incompatible with GPL-2.0-only because of its patent and
indemnity terms, which is what makes the dual expression useful rather than merely conventional; its
express patent grant is worth having where algorithm patents on point cloud segmentation and
classification are not hypothetical.

**MPL-2.0** was seriously considered, particularly for the algorithms crate. Its file-level copyleft
would let a proprietary product link the crate while requiring improvements to its own files to be
published, and section 3.3 makes it GPL/LGPL-compatible so QGIS and CloudCompare remain eligible. It
has a patent grant. Servo and WebRender are Rust precedents; Eigen is the C++ precedent of an MPL
numerics library used inside proprietary products. Its problem is that "file" is not a well-defined
unit in Rust: the compilation unit is the crate, and inlining and monomorphisation cross that boundary
freely, with no settled interpretation of what file-scope copyleft then covers. It also requires a
downstream legal review that Apache-2.0 does not.

**LGPL-3.0** was rejected on mechanical grounds. Its central mechanism is the section 4 relink
requirement, which presumes dynamic linking; Rust has no stable ABI and links statically by default,
so compliance would mean shipping object files or a build environment. Generic code monomorphises into
the consumer's binary, so the boundary the licence depends on is not a location in a Rust program.

**GPL-3.0** on the libraries would foreclose the adoption goal outright, excluding PDAL and GDAL.

A commercial relicensing model — AGPL plus paid exceptions — was noted as coherent but requires the
project to hold assignable copyright, hence a contributor licence agreement, which changes how
contributions are taken from the first commit. No commercial driver was present.

## Decision

The licence splits at the crate boundary: library crates `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`, applications
`AGPL-3.0-or-later`, contributions inbound-equals-outbound. The obligations are written in
[RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) and [RFC-0001:C-CONTRIB](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-contrib); this ADR records only *why*.

Why **permissive libraries**:

- **Adoption is the point.** The tools that would adopt them cannot link copyleft: PDAL is BSD-3,
  GDAL is MIT. A copyleft library would be adoptable by less than half the ecosystem, and the excluded
  half is the half whose adoption makes these crates infrastructure rather than a fourth
  reimplementation.
- **`Apache-2.0 OR MIT`, not Apache alone.** Apache-2.0 is incompatible with GPL-2.0-*only*; MIT is
  the escape hatch. Apache stays in the pair for its express patent grant.
- **The GDAL precedent.** Permissive libraries get appropriated and also become the substrate the
  field is built on. That is the position `strider-core` should want.

Why **copyleft application**, and why AGPL rather than GPL:

- **It blocks the threat that is real.** Nobody profits by lifting one estimator; the risk is a
  proprietary repackaging of the whole workbench, which copyleft on the application prevents.
- **AGPL is free insurance.** Its network clause never fires for a locally-run binary, so on the
  desktop it is identical to GPL — while a hosted or browser component later is already covered,
  without a second licence and a one-directional compatibility rule between them.
- **Qt points the same way.** Qt's open-source terms are LGPL-3.0/GPL-3.0, so a GPL-family
  application licence is the natural fit regardless.

Why **MPL-2.0 is deferred, not rejected on merit**: it is the right licence and the right tier if any
crate ever takes copyleft, but file-scope copyleft has no settled meaning in generic-heavy Rust, and
that ambiguity would sit under the most valuable code.

Why **no CLA**: inbound-equals-outbound minimises contribution friction. The consequence — no
unilateral relicensing, and no open-core or sell-exceptions model — is accepted knowingly and written
into [RFC-0001:C-CONTRIB](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-contrib) (2) rather than left to be discovered.

## Consequences

### Positive

PDAL, GDAL, QGIS, CloudCompare and commercial products can all adopt the libraries, which is the
precondition for the spatial access layer and format adapters becoming shared infrastructure. Contribution
friction is minimal, plugin authors are unconstrained in their own licensing, and the application consumes
its own libraries without friction because permissive flows into copyleft.

### Negative

Two licence regimes in one workspace — correct per-crate declarations, REUSE headers, and automated
dependency-licence enforcement that must actually be wired up rather than intended. A contributor who adds
a copyleft dependency to a library crate has introduced a licensing defect no ordinary test would catch.

Reciprocity from library users is given up. A proprietary forestry product can build on the spatial access
layer, adapters and algorithms and return nothing. [RFC-0001:C-CONTRIB](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-contrib) additionally forecloses open-core
and sell-exceptions models, and that cost grows with every merge, since contributions already accepted stay
unassigned regardless of later policy.

### Neutral

The appropriation this permits is what happened to GDAL and PROJ, and also why they are the substrate the
field is built on — so whether it reads as a cost depends entirely on whether adoption materialises.

Watch for a library crate acquiring a copyleft dependency **transitively** through a minor version bump.
That is the concrete failure mode of this decision, it is silent, and it is why [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4
requires automated verification on every dependency change.

Reversal cost is asymmetric. Adding copyleft to a *new* crate later is easy. Relicensing an existing crate
needs every contributor's consent and becomes impractical in the low tens of contributors. Making libraries
*more* permissive is not possible at all once they are copyleft — the direction this decision deliberately
avoids needing.

## Alternatives Considered

### Split at the crate boundary: library crates Apache-2.0 OR MIT, applications AGPL-3.0-or-later, contributions inbound-equals-outbound (accepted)

- **Pros:** Libraries adoptable by PDAL, GDAL, QGIS, CloudCompare and commercial tools alike, Copyleft still prevents the threat that matters: proprietary repackaging of the whole workbench, Apache's patent grant covers a field with real algorithm patents; MIT keeps GPL-2.0-only consumers eligible, Permissive-to-copyleft is a one-way door left open: the application consumes its own libraries freely, Matches where value accrues — the product, not any individual estimator
- **Cons:** A proprietary product can build on the libraries and contribute nothing back, Two licence regimes to document and enforce across one workspace

### AGPL-3.0 throughout, libraries included (rejected)

- **Pros:** Strongest reciprocity: every downstream use must publish source, One licence, no per-crate rules to enforce or explain, Consistent with the copyleft culture of QGIS and CloudCompare
- **Cons:** PDAL (BSD-3) and GDAL (MIT) cannot link it at all, AGPL-3.0 is incompatible with GPL-2.0, so QGIS and CloudCompare are excluded too, The network-use clause is inert for a desktop application, so the adoption cost buys nothing, Plugin authors would have to be AGPL, constraining an extension ecosystem before it exists
- **Rejected because:** It excludes the entire ecosystem it was chosen to belong to. A tool positioned as the QGIS of point clouds would be unusable by QGIS, because AGPL-3.0 and GPL-2.0 are incompatible, and unusable by PDAL and GDAL because they are permissive. The clause that distinguishes AGPL from GPL never fires for a desktop binary, so the full cost is paid for no benefit.

### MPL-2.0 for the algorithms crate, permissive for the rest (rejected)

- **Pros:** File-level copyleft returns improvements to the algorithms while permitting proprietary linking, Section 3.3 keeps GPL and LGPL consumers eligible; has an express patent grant, Copyleft applied exactly where the differentiated work is, and nowhere else, Established precedent: Servo and WebRender in Rust, Eigen in C++
- **Cons:** MPL file-scope has no settled meaning in Rust, where the compilation unit is the crate, Requires a downstream legal review that Apache-2.0 does not, A mixed-licence workspace needs per-crate enforcement and confuses contributors
- **Rejected because:** Deferred rather than wrong. The reasoning is sound and this is the right tier if any crate gets copyleft, but file-scope copyleft is undefined for generic-heavy Rust, and that uncertainty would sit under the crate holding the project's most valuable code. Adopting it later for new crates is possible; retracting it is not.

### LGPL-3.0 for the library crates (rejected)

- **Pros:** Copyleft on the libraries while nominally permitting proprietary linking, Familiar to the Qt ecosystem, whose own open-source terms include LGPL-3.0
- **Cons:** Section 4's relink requirement presumes dynamic linking; Rust has no stable ABI and links statically, Generic code monomorphises into the consumer's binary, so the library boundary is not a location, Compliance would mean shipping object files or a full build environment
- **Rejected because:** Mechanically inapplicable to Rust rather than merely unattractive. The licence's operative mechanism assumes a boundary that does not exist in a statically linked, monomorphising language, and there is no settled interpretation to rely on. Adopting it would put unresolvable ambiguity underneath the project's foundation.
